exampleProvenance: Original fictional teaching examples; no published-source quotations or official rubric claims.

guides.title: Start with a purpose
guides.explanation: Before you plan, name what this piece is trying to do for a reader. A task can ask you to explain, interpret, argue, reflect or tell a story. Your first decision is not the number of paragraphs; it is the understanding you want the reader to reach.
guides.workedExample: Vague starting point: “This is about belonging.” More focused purpose: “I want to explore how being given a useful role can change someone’s sense of belonging.” The second version gives you a direction for selecting details without dictating a final essay structure.
guides.practice: Write one sentence beginning “I want my reader to understand…” Then identify one detail that could help you show it.

guides.title: Develop a working interpretation
guides.explanation: A working interpretation connects a specific observation to a larger idea. It is allowed to change as you read and draft. A topic labels an area; an interpretation explains what you think the material suggests.
guides.workedExample: Topic: “The empty chair.” Interpretation: “By returning to the empty chair after the celebration, the narrator makes absence more noticeable than it was in the crowded room.” This identifies a choice and explains its effect. It is an original fictional example, not a quotation from a text.
guides.practice: Name one choice in your text or subject. Explain what that choice makes a reader notice, question or understand.

guides.title: Develop a paragraph
guides.explanation: A paragraph needs a clear purpose, relevant detail and enough explanation for the reader to follow your thinking. These are useful functions, not a required sentence formula. Sometimes the detail comes first; sometimes the claim does.
guides.workedExample: Point: an invitation changes the character’s role. Detail: another speaker asks for the character’s opinion rather than simply offering a seat. Explanation: the character is treated as someone whose contribution matters. Notice how the explanation adds a meaning the detail does not state on its own.
guides.practice: Find one paragraph in your draft. Label its purpose, detail and explanation. Add what the reader still needs, rather than adding sentences only for length.

guides.title: Choose and record evidence
guides.explanation: Useful evidence is specific and relevant to the idea you are developing. Record the source and locator while you have it open. A paraphrase restates an idea; it is not a direct quotation and should not be dressed up as one.
guides.workedExample: Unhelpful note: “The character is lonely.” More useful note: “After the meeting, the character waits by the door while the others continue talking.” The second note gives you a precise moment to analyze. It is a fictional scene description, not exact quoted language.
guides.practice: Add one evidence card. Label it Quote, Paraphrase, Scene, Personal example or Other, then write why it matters to your point.

guides.title: Move beyond summary
guides.explanation: Summary explains what happens. Analysis explains how a choice, detail or relationship contributes to meaning. Begin with a precise observation, then make the connection visible for the reader.
guides.workedExample: Summary: “The character keeps the broken key.” Analysis: “Keeping a key that no longer opens the door suggests the character is attached to what the home represented, not merely to entering the building.” The explanation connects an object and an action to an idea. It does not just repeat the event.
guides.practice: Underline one sentence that only tells what happened. Add a sentence explaining what that particular detail suggests and why.

guides.title: Integrate a quotation carefully
guides.explanation: Introduce a quotation so the reader knows why it is present. Keep quoted words exact, show omissions or changes appropriately for the required style and record a locator. Explain the relevant language rather than assuming the quotation proves the point by itself.
guides.workedExample: Original fictional wording: “The hall swallowed her answer.” A writer could introduce it as an image that makes the speaker seem unheard, then discuss the verb “swallowed”. This is a made-up teaching example; do not cite it as a real published source.
guides.practice: Choose a quotation you have verified. Write an introduction to it and explain one specific word or choice. Check your assignment’s citation instructions.

guides.title: Give the reader a starting point
guides.explanation: An opening should give the reader enough context and a reason to follow the piece. It does not need a grand statement about all of humanity. The right opening depends on purpose, form and audience.
guides.workedExample: Broad: “People have always wanted to belong.” More concrete: “No one moved the spare chair until someone asked for her opinion.” The concrete opening raises a useful question and introduces a moment the writer can develop. Both sentences are original examples, not required templates.
guides.practice: Try two opening approaches for your project: one direct statement of the problem and one precise moment. Choose the one that best suits your purpose.

guides.title: Choose a meaningful order
guides.explanation: Order should help the reader build an understanding. Chronological order can suit a narrative; an argument may move from a shared concern to reasons, complications and a conclusion. Do not arrange sections only because a template gives them numbers.
guides.workedExample: A reflection could move from feeling out of place, to a specific invitation, to a changed understanding. Each step changes what the reader knows. Repeating three unrelated examples of loneliness may not create the same development.
guides.practice: Write a one-line purpose for each section. Move or remove a section whose role is unclear; explain why the new order works.

guides.title: Make a moment do work
guides.explanation: A narrative detail should help the reader experience the scene or understand a change. You do not need to describe everything. Select actions, objects, dialogue and sensory details that support the focus of the story.
guides.workedExample: Instead of listing the room’s furniture, a writer might focus on a character smoothing the same folded invitation before speaking. That action can suggest uncertainty without naming the emotion directly. It is an original fictional example.
guides.practice: Choose one important moment in your narrative. Add a specific action or object that helps show what the moment means.

guides.title: Choose precise language
guides.explanation: Voice comes from choices that suit your purpose and reader, not from using the longest words available. Precision often means replacing a vague noun or verb with a more exact one while keeping your own way of expressing the idea.
guides.workedExample: Vague: “The event had a big impact.” More precise: “After the meeting, she volunteered to lead the next discussion.” The second sentence shows a change the reader can understand. You may still need to explain its significance.
guides.practice: Find three vague words in your draft. Replace only those that hide meaning; do not force a thesaurus word into a clear sentence.

guides.title: Revise in focused passes
guides.explanation: Trying to fix every problem at once can make revision hard to direct. Begin with meaning and structure, then look at evidence/explanation, then style and conventions. A strong sentence is not useful if the paragraph no longer belongs in the piece.
guides.workedExample: First pass: notice that two paragraphs repeat the same point. Second pass: combine the strongest details and add the missing explanation. Final pass: check sentence boundaries and punctuation in the revised paragraph. The order avoids polishing text that you later remove.
guides.practice: Choose one revision pass. Make one change you can explain, then record what the change helps your reader understand.

guides.title: Turn feedback into an action
guides.explanation: Feedback becomes useful when you connect it to a concrete revision decision. Record the feedback accurately, identify the part of the draft it concerns and decide what to try. You can ask for clarification when the next step is unclear.
guides.workedExample: Feedback: “Explain this more.” Possible action: identify the claim and detail, then add the missing connection between them. The goal is not automatically to make the paragraph longer; it is to make the reasoning clearer. This feedback is fictional.
guides.practice: Add one feedback note you received. Write a specific next action and mark it addressed only after reviewing the result.
